newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians wade ashore from derelict refugee ship.
newsitem.headline: Albanians wade ashore from derelict refugee ship.

text.p: About 100 Albanians were rescued on Tuesday when the derelict freighter they had commandeered to take them to Italy ran aground south of the port of Durres.
The would-be refugees waded ashore through breaking waves and a stiff breeze at Golame Beach after being ferried off the rusty coaster by motorised rubber dinghies.
"I am defeated, finished," gasped 30-year old Mohamed Backa as he stumbled onto the beach, drenched and shivering.
"This boat was my last hope. I thought I could get to Italy but now I am going back to Tirana. The port is blocked. There's just no way to escape."
The would-be refugees had relied on improvised paddles, sea currents and sails fashioned from trash bags to launch the freighter from the port of Durres on Tuesday morning.

The ship had been tied up at the port for several days but Albanians had doubted its seaworthiness because it had no power. Lacking any other means to flee they finally used ropes to pull it along the dock and pushed off into the current. The boat was so overloaded and low in the water that passengers were able to use bits of lumber and metal sheeting as paddles to propel the craft out of the harbour.
About half of the people on board disembarked at the mouth of the harbour for fear the boat might sink. The remainder drifted out into the Adriatic to what they hoped would be a better life abroad.

The voyage, which began about 0830 on Tuesday morning, was a short one. Carried by wind and currents the ship ran aground five hours later about a kilometre (half a mile) off Golame Beach, which is 10 Km (six miles) south of Durres centre.
Uniformed civil police watching the rescue from a van parked on the beach said that they were supervising the effort. Civilians in the area insisted the police were doing nothing but watching.
Sami Kola, 40, stood on the beach with his arm around his young daughter squinting out into the Adriatic and marking the progress of the rescue.
"Until one year ago I was an army officer, but now I am just another person trying to get out of Albania," he said.

"This problem we are facing is an economic problem, not a political problem. What difference does it make who is in the government if no one has a job? It's not just that people have lost money. No one can make a living here."

The recent collapse of nine pyramid schemes in Albania bankrupted many families and has led to civil unrest, especially in the south. Thousands of people are trying to flee to Italy from the country's Adriatic ports and beaches.
Sami Kola's daughter Luciana, 12, looked away as men emerged from the low surf wearing only underpants.
"We lived not far from here in Kavaje until five days ago and already I miss my friends," she said, ducking the wind-whipped sand and salt spray.
"We are living in the forest here waiting for a boat. My parents say I must be brave and go with them to Italy because they have no jobs here."

As she finished speaking a refugee emerged from the sea and stood dripping in his underwear on the beach. Holding one soaked shoe in each hand, arms opened wide in disgust, he exclaimed: "This is what it means to be an Albanian."
